# Strata — Product Requirements Document

**Version:** 1.0
**Date:** August 15, 2026
**Author:** Generated by Claude
**Status:** Draft — pending review

---

## 1. Overview

### 1.1 Problem Statement

Most work-management tools assume work is a flat list of tasks with a few optional custom fields. Real work at most teams past a certain size is not flat — it is a structured hierarchy with repeating shape:

- An **agency** runs 40 clients × 6 recurring deliverable types × 12 months. That's ~2,900 items a year, each with client-specific fields (brand guidelines link, approval contact, SLA tier) that differ by deliverable type.
- A **product marketing team** runs one campaign that exists in 14 regional variants. Thirteen of the fields are identical across regions; three differ (local launch date, localized asset link, regional budget).
- An **ops team** tracks equipment, contracts, and locations in the same system. A "Contract" has renewal date, counterparty, and value. A "Location" has square footage, lease expiry, and site manager. Nothing about those two record types is shared except that both are work.

Today these teams have three bad options:

| Option | What breaks |
|---|---|
| **Monday / ClickUp** | Custom fields are per-board and untyped-ish. There is no reusable schema, no inheritance, and no bulk-editing story past a few dozen rows. Teams duplicate boards, copy-paste rows by hand, and discover six months later that half the records are missing data nobody noticed. |
| **Jira** | Real hierarchy exists (epic → story → subtask) but is fixed-depth, developer-shaped, and administered through a settings UI that a marketing lead will not touch. Custom field configuration is a Jira-admin task, not a team task. |
| **Akeneo (PIM)** | Has exactly the right data model — families, attribute groups, category trees, product models with variant inheritance, completeness scoring. It is also, by broad consensus among its own users, painful to set up and administer, requires technical staff, and is built for product catalogs rather than work. |

The gap: **nobody has taken the PIM data model and made it usable by a non-technical team, inside a work-management tool.**

The cost of the gap is measurable and mundane. Teams spend hours a week on manual duplication, they cannot answer "which of our 300 deliverables are missing a required field," and they hit a ceiling where the tool that got them to 20 people actively obstructs them at 60.

### 1.2 Proposed Solution

Strata is a web-based work-management platform. It looks and feels like Monday or ClickUp — boards, lists, saved views, a familiar sidebar — but underneath it runs a real structured data model borrowed from PIM tooling: reusable **Item Types** with typed fields organized into groups, **category trees** that classify items independently of the work hierarchy, **variant inheritance** so a parent item's shared fields flow down to per-region children, and a visible **completeness score** that surfaces missing data before it becomes a problem.

The bet is that the data model is not the hard part — making it approachable is. So the product's center of gravity is the **grid view**: a spreadsheet-grade editing surface with inline cells, multi-select, copy/paste to and from Excel, fill-down, and undo, over hundreds of structured items. Everything a team would otherwise do by hand across dozens of cards, they do in one grid in one pass, with a preview of what's about to change and a one-click undo after.

### 1.3 Goals

**Primary goal:** A non-technical team member can define a structured Item Type with custom fields and start working with hundreds of items of that type — bulk-editing, importing, filtering, reparenting — without a schema editor, an admin ticket, or any code.

**Secondary goals:**

1. **Make hierarchy legible.** A user can see and navigate three independent axes (work hierarchy, category trees, variants) without confusing them.
2. **Make gaps visible.** Every item and every view surfaces how complete it is, so missing data is caught in the tool rather than in a client meeting.
3. **Make bulk operations safe.** Every multi-item change is previewed before it commits and reversible after, so people stop being afraid of the bulk tools.
4. **Make performance a feature.** Filter and search stay under half a second at 100k items per workspace, because a tool that models complexity and then chokes on it has solved nothing.

### 1.4 Non-Goals

Strata v1 explicitly does **not** try to:

- **Reach feature parity with Monday/ClickUp/Jira.** No sprints, no burndown charts, no time tracking, no docs/wiki, no chat. Strata competes on data modeling, not on breadth.
- **Ship a native mobile app.** Responsive down to tablet; phones get a read-mostly experience.
- **Be an integrations platform.** A documented REST API and webhooks in v1. Slack, GitHub, and calendar sync are Phase 2.
- **Include AI features.** Not in MVP scope. See §5 Phase 2 for two candidates.
- **Serve regulated industries.** No SOC 2, HIPAA, or FedRAMP posture in v1. This constrains the addressable market on purpose.
- **Replace a real PIM.** No product syndication, no channel publishing, no DAM. Strata borrows Akeneo's ideas, it does not compete with Akeneo's job.

## 2. Target Users

### 2.1 Primary Persona — "The Ops-Minded Operator"

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Who** | Agency operations lead, marketing ops manager, or business ops generalist at a 20–150 person company. Owns the tooling but is not an engineer. |
| **Pain** | She is the person who built the current Monday board and is now the only one who understands it. She spends 3–5 hours a week duplicating recurring work, hand-fixing rows, and chasing people for missing fields. She has been told Jira "would fix this" and has looked at it once. |
| **Goal** | Set up a structure once that holds up as the team grows, and stop being the human integration layer. |
| **Context** | Desktop, 2–4 hours a day in the tool, often with a spreadsheet open beside it. Lives in bulk operations and saved views. |
| **Tech savvy** | High for a non-engineer. Fluent in Excel (pivot tables, VLOOKUP), comfortable with the idea of a "field type," will not write SQL or edit YAML. |

**Why she matters:** she is both the buyer and the admin. If Item Type creation takes her more than a few minutes or feels like a database tool, the product is dead at first contact — this is precisely where Akeneo loses non-technical teams.

### 2.2 Secondary Persona — "The Contributor"

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Who** | Designer, writer, account manager, or coordinator doing the actual work. 5–20 people per workspace. |
| **Pain** | Doesn't care about the data model at all. Wants to know what's assigned to them, update status, and not be nagged. |
| **Goal** | Open the tool, see my work, change a few things, close the tool. |
| **Context** | Board or list view, 15–30 minutes a day, occasionally on a tablet. |
| **Tech savvy** | Medium. Has used Monday or Asana. Will bounce off anything that looks like a schema. |

**How their needs differ:** the Contributor should be able to use Strata for months without ever learning what a variant is. Every advanced concept must be invisible by default and only surface when it's already relevant to something in front of them.

### 2.3 Tertiary Persona — "The Client / External Stakeholder"

Guest-role user, invited to a scoped slice of a category tree. Read-mostly, sees a curated field subset via a shared view, reviews and updates the handful of fields they've been granted. Matters because agency workflows are the sharpest wedge use case, and "can I show this to my client without showing them our internal margin field" is a purchase-blocking question.

> ⚠️ **Assumption:** The wedge market is agencies and marketing/ops teams in the 20–150 person band. If early research shows the sharper pain is in the ops/structured-records use case (equipment, contracts, locations), the persona ordering and onboarding presets should be revisited before build starts.

## 3. Core Concepts

Before requirements, the vocabulary. These names appear identically in the Tech Spec, API Design, and UI. **Getting these names right in the product is a primary UX risk** — see §6.

| Concept | Definition | Akeneo analogue |
|---|---|---|
| **Workspace** | The tenant. Hard data isolation boundary. Has members, roles, billing. | — |
| **Item** | The atomic unit. A task, a deliverable, a campaign, a contract, a piece of equipment. | Product |
| **Item Type** | Reusable template defining which fields an item has, which are required, and how they're grouped. | Family |
| **Field** | A typed attribute definition. 14 types in v1 — enumerated in §4.1. Belongs to an Item Type. | Attribute |
| **Field Group** | Named section that fields belong to, so the detail view isn't one 40-field wall. | Attribute group |
| **Work hierarchy** | Parent/child nesting of items. Arbitrary depth. The "project → deliverable → subtask" axis. | — |
| **Category Tree** | A named, nested classification. Items belong to zero or more nodes, across multiple trees at once. Independent of the work hierarchy. | Category tree |
| **Variant Model** | An item that acts as a template for its variants. Owns the shared field values. | Product model |
| **Variant** | A child of a Variant Model that inherits shared fields and overrides only the fields on its variant axis. | Product variant |
| **Variant Axis** | The field(s) that define what varies — e.g. "Region," "Channel." Defined on the Item Type. | Variation axis |
| **Completeness** | % of an item's required fields that are filled. Shown on the item and aggregated in views. | Completeness |
| **View** | A saved configuration: view type (grid/list/board), filters, sort, visible field subset, grouping. Shareable. | Channel/locale (loosely) |
| **Change Set** | An atomic, previewable, undoable batch of item mutations. Also the audit record. | — |
| **Import Profile** | A saved CSV/Excel column-to-field mapping, reusable across imports. | Import job profile |

**The three axes, stated plainly**, because this is the concept most likely to confuse a Monday/ClickUp switcher:

```
Work hierarchy    — "what is part of what"       Q3 Launch  →  Landing Page  →  Copy review
Category trees    — "how do we classify it"      Q3 Launch is in [Client: Acme] and [Product Line: Widgets]
Variants          — "what version of it"         Q3 Launch  →  Q3 Launch (EMEA), Q3 Launch (APAC)
```

An item participates in all three simultaneously and independently.

## 4. User Stories & Requirements

### 4.1 Item Type Builder

> As an ops lead, I want to define a reusable Item Type with my own fields in under two minutes, so that I can model my team's actual work without a database tool or an admin request.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] Creating an Item Type from a starter preset ("Task," "Client Project," "Campaign," "Product Variant," "Structured Record," "Blank") takes ≤ 2 minutes end-to-end, measured from "New Item Type" click to first item created. This is a **gating metric**, not an aspiration.
- [ ] The default creation flow shows: name, icon/color, and a field list. Nothing else.
- [ ] Field creation is one row: name + type picker. Type-specific config (select options, number precision, relation target) expands inline only after a type is chosen.
- [ ] Supported field types in v1: `text`, `long_text`, `number`, `date`, `datetime`, `select`, `multi_select`, `checkbox`, `url`, `email`, `user`, `relation` (to another item), `currency`, `percent`.
- [ ] Field groups, variant axes, completeness requirements, and per-field permissions live behind an **Advanced** toggle that is collapsed by default and remembers state per user.
- [ ] Renaming a field never breaks stored data — fields have an immutable `key` and a mutable `label`.
- [ ] Changing a field's type is allowed with an explicit conversion preview showing how many values will convert cleanly, how many will be coerced, and how many will be preserved as unparsed text. Nothing is silently destroyed.
- [ ] Deleting a field soft-deletes for 30 days with a restore path. Values are retained during that window.
- [ ] An Item Type in use by ≥ 1 item cannot have a required field added without either a default value or an explicit "leave existing items incomplete" acknowledgment.

### 4.2 Grid View (the hero surface)

> As an ops lead, I want to edit hundreds of items in a spreadsheet-style grid, so that I stop copy-pasting between Excel and my PM tool.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] Inline cell editing: click to select, type to replace, Enter to commit and move down, Tab to commit and move right, Esc to cancel.
- [ ] Full keyboard navigation: arrows, Ctrl/Cmd+arrows to jump to edges, Shift+arrows to extend selection, Ctrl/Cmd+A to select all loaded rows.
- [ ] Multi-cell rectangular selection with a visible selection border and a count readout ("42 cells, 12 rows").
- [ ] Copy (`Ctrl/Cmd+C`) writes TSV to the clipboard, pasteable directly into Excel and Google Sheets with types preserved as text.
- [ ] Paste (`Ctrl/Cmd+V`) from Excel/Sheets maps clipboard TSV onto the selection rectangle, coerces per column type, and shows a preview of any values that will not convert before committing.
- [ ] Fill-down (`Ctrl/Cmd+D`) and fill-handle drag on the selection's bottom-right corner.
- [ ] Undo (`Ctrl/Cmd+Z`) and redo (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Z`) across at least the last 50 operations in the session, including bulk operations.
- [ ] Column reorder by drag, column resize, column pin (freeze) for the first N columns.
- [ ] Row grouping by any field, with collapsible groups and per-group aggregates (count, sum, avg, % complete).
- [ ] Virtualized rendering: scrolling 10,000 loaded rows stays at 60fps on a 2020-era laptop.
- [ ] A completeness column is available in every grid and shows a compact bar + %.
- [ ] Validation errors render inline in the cell with a specific message ("Expected a number — got 'TBD'") and **never block saving the rest of the row**. Invalid values persist as flagged drafts on the field.

### 4.3 Bulk Operations & Undo

> As an ops lead, I want to see exactly what a bulk edit will change before it commits, so that I trust the tool enough to actually use it on 300 rows.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] Every operation affecting > 1 item routes through a **Change Set** with a preview step.
- [ ] The preview shows: number of items affected, per-field before → after, a sample of up to 20 affected rows, and a count of items that will be skipped (with reasons — permission, validation, locked).
- [ ] Commit is explicit. The preview is not auto-applied on a timer.
- [ ] After commit, a persistent toast offers **Undo** for 60 seconds; the change set also remains undoable from the activity feed for 24 hours.
- [ ] Undo restores prior values for every field the change set touched, and is itself recorded as a change set (undo is auditable, not a hole in history).
- [ ] Supported bulk operations in v1 — eight: `set_field`, `clear_field`, `change_type` (with field-mapping preview), `reparent` in the work hierarchy, `tree_assign`, `tree_unassign`, `delete`, `assign_user`. (A ninth change-set operation, `create`, backs single-item creation and import commits but is not exposed as a bulk action.)
- [ ] Bulk operations on > 500 items run as a background job with progress, and the UI stays usable.

### 4.4 Import & Export

> As an ops lead, I want to import a spreadsheet and save the column mapping, so that next month's import takes ten seconds instead of ten minutes.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] Upload CSV or XLSX. Header row auto-detected; first 20 rows previewed.
- [ ] Column mapping UI suggests target fields by fuzzy name match, with a confidence indicator; the user confirms or overrides each.
- [ ] Mapping configurations save as named **Import Profiles**, re-selectable on the next import.
- [ ] A dry-run validation report runs before any write: row count, new vs. matched-existing (via a chosen match key), per-column type coercion warnings, and a downloadable error CSV.
- [ ] Import commits as a single Change Set and is undoable like any other.
- [ ] Export respects the current view — its filters, sort, visible fields, and grouping — and offers CSV or XLSX.
- [ ] Export of > 5,000 rows runs as a background job with an email/notification link to the file.

### 4.5 Category Trees

> As an ops lead, I want to classify items into more than one tree at once, so that I can slice by client and by product line without duplicating anything.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] A workspace has one built-in tree plus at least one user-created custom tree in v1.
- [ ] Trees support arbitrary nesting depth; nodes are drag-reorderable and drag-reparentable.
- [ ] An item can belong to multiple nodes within one tree and to nodes in multiple trees simultaneously.
- [ ] Selecting a node filters to that node's items; a toggle includes/excludes descendant nodes.
- [ ] Assigning items to nodes works by drag from grid/list onto the tree, and as a bulk operation.
- [ ] Deleting a node asks what to do with its items (unassign / move to parent / move to chosen node) and never silently orphans them.
- [ ] Tree membership is visible on the item detail panel as removable chips.

### 4.6 Variants

> As a marketing lead, I want per-region versions of a campaign that inherit the shared fields, so that changing the tagline once updates all fourteen regions.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] An Item Type can declare one or more **variant axes** (e.g. Region, Channel), each backed by a `select` field.
- [ ] Each field on a variant-enabled Item Type is marked **shared** (owned by the model, inherited read-only by variants) or **variant-level** (owned independently by each variant).
- [ ] Creating a Variant Model and generating variants across an axis is a single guided action: pick axis values → preview the N variants that will be created → create.
- [ ] A variant displays inherited values with a distinct visual treatment and an "inherited from [model]" affordance.
- [ ] Overriding an inherited value on a variant is explicit (an "override" action), and the override is visually marked with a one-click "revert to inherited."
- [ ] Editing a shared field on the model propagates to all non-overridden variants, and the change set preview states how many variants will be affected.
- [ ] Completeness is computed per variant, using its effective (inherited + overridden) values.
- [ ] **v1 constraint:** an item cannot be both a Variant Model and a work-hierarchy parent. Variants do not have their own work-hierarchy children. This keeps the mental model teachable; revisit in Phase 2.

### 4.7 Completeness

> As an ops lead, I want to see at a glance which items are missing required data, so that I catch gaps before a client does.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] Fields are individually markable as required-for-completeness on their Item Type.
- [ ] An item's completeness = (filled required fields ÷ total required fields), displayed as a % and a bar.
- [ ] Completeness is recomputed on every write and is filterable and sortable like any field.
- [ ] The item detail panel lists exactly which required fields are missing, each as a click-to-focus link.
- [ ] Views show an aggregate completeness for the filtered set and per group when grouped.
- [ ] A saved view can filter on "incomplete only" as a one-click preset.

### 4.8 Views (Grid / List / Board / Detail)

> As a contributor, I want a board of just my work, so that I never have to think about the data model.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] Three view types in v1 over the same underlying data: **grid**, **list**, **board (Kanban)**. Switching view type preserves filters and sort.
- [ ] Views save with a name, an owner, and a visibility setting (private / workspace / shared-with-guests).
- [ ] A view stores: type, filters, sort, visible field subset, group-by, and per-column width/order.
- [ ] Board view groups by any `select` or `user` field; drag between columns writes the field value.
- [ ] Filters compose with AND/OR groups across any field, including completeness, tree membership, and hierarchy depth.
- [ ] The item detail panel opens over any view (side panel on desktop, full screen on tablet) and shows fields organized by field group, completeness, work-hierarchy breadcrumb, tree chips, variant relationship, and activity.
- [ ] A view shared with a Guest exposes only its visible field subset. **This is a presentation control, not a security boundary — see §9 Risk 3.**

### 4.9 Permissions & Admin

> As a workspace owner, I want an agency client to see only their own slice, so that I can invite them without a separate tool.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] Roles: **Owner**, **Admin**, **Member**, **Guest**, **Viewer**.
- [ ] Owner: everything, including billing and workspace deletion. Admin: everything except billing. Member: create/edit items, create views; cannot change Item Types or trees. Guest: scoped to specific category tree nodes, read plus edit on explicitly granted fields — no create, no delete, no bulk tools, no API access. Viewer: read-only across the workspace.
- [ ] Workspace data isolation is enforced at the database layer, not only in application code.
- [ ] Guest scoping is by category tree node, with descendants included.
- [ ] Every permission-denied action produces a specific message, never a silent no-op or a blank screen.

### 4.10 Notifications & Activity

- [ ] Per-item activity feed showing every change set that touched it, who, when, and the before → after.
- [ ] Workspace activity feed, filterable by user, item type, and date.
- [ ] Email notifications for: assignment, guest invitation, import completed, and export ready. Batched digest option. (Mentions are deferred with comments — see §10.)
- [ ] In-app notification center with unread state.

### Out of Scope

| Feature | Reason |
|---|---|
| Native iOS/Android apps | Primary persona is desktop-bound. Responsive web to tablet covers the contributor. |
| Deep third-party integrations | API + webhooks let early adopters self-serve; each native integration is weeks of ongoing maintenance. |
| AI features | Would distract from the differentiator and add cost/latency before product-market fit. |
| SOC 2 / HIPAA / enterprise compliance | 6+ months and meaningful spend for a market segment v1 isn't targeting. |
| Time tracking, sprints, docs, chat | Breadth is Monday's game. Strata wins on depth of model or not at all. |
| More than one custom category tree | Proves the multi-tree model without the UI complexity of arbitrary tree management. |

## 6. The Priority: User-Friendly Data Handling

This section is a first-class requirement, not a design nicety. Strata's entire thesis is that the PIM data model is correct and its usability is not. If Strata ships the model and repeats the usability failure, it is Akeneo with better colors.

### 6.1 Progressive disclosure

**Requirement:** every advanced concept is invisible until relevant.

- Item Type creation defaults to: name, icon, fields. That's the whole screen.
- **Advanced** (collapsed by default) contains: field groups, variant axes, completeness requirements, field-level permissions, API key/slug.
- Starter presets ship with sensible fields already populated. "Client Project" arrives with Client, Owner, Due Date, Status, Budget — not an empty schema editor.
- A user never sees the word "variant," "axis," or "completeness" until they have either enabled it or encountered an item that uses it.
- Empty states teach. The zero-state of the tree manager explains what a second tree is *for*, with a concrete example, not just a "Create tree" button.

**Measurable gate:** median time from "New Item Type" to first item created ≤ 2 minutes for a user who has never seen the product. Tested in moderated usability sessions before launch, n ≥ 5.

### 6.2 Grid view is a first-class citizen

Not a table with editable cells — a spreadsheet. The bar is Airtable and Google Sheets, and users will compare it to those within thirty seconds. The full interaction contract is in §4.2 and specified key-by-key in the UI/UX Notes. Three points bear repeating:

- **Clipboard interop with Excel is mandatory, both directions.** The primary persona has a spreadsheet open right now. If paste-from-Excel doesn't work, the product hasn't solved her problem.
- **Undo covers bulk operations,** not just single-cell edits. Undo that silently declines to reverse the risky thing is worse than no undo.
- **Rendering performance is part of the feature.** A grid that stutters at 5,000 rows reads as broken regardless of correctness.

### 6.3 Preview before, undo after

Every operation touching more than one item shows what will change before it changes, and is reversible after. No exceptions, including imports and item-type conversions. The reasoning is behavioral: bulk tools in existing PM products are under-used because users have been burned once and now edit 300 rows by hand. Preview + undo is what converts the feature from "technically present" to "actually used."

### 6.4 Validation is inline, specific, and non-blocking

- Specific: "Expected a number — got 'TBD'." Never "Invalid input."
- Positioned at the cell or field, not in a summary banner at the top.
- **Never blocks saving the rest of the item.** A bad value in one field is stored as a flagged draft on that field while every other field commits. Data entry is interrupted work; forcing all-or-nothing saves loses real user input.
- Import validation is a pre-flight report with a downloadable error CSV, not a wall of red at row 4,000.

### 6.5 Search and filter stay fast under real load

Explicit product requirement, restated as an engineering budget in the Tech Spec:

| Operation | Target (p95) | At scale |
|---|---|---|
| Filtered + sorted page load (100 rows) | < 300 ms server | 100k items / workspace |
| Keystroke → filtered results rendered | < 500 ms | 100k items / workspace |
| Text search across items | < 400 ms | 100k items / workspace |
| Subtree filter (node + all descendants) | < 300 ms | tree depth 8, 50k items in subtree |
| Bulk update commit, 500 items | < 3 s | synchronous path |
| Grid scroll | 60 fps | 10k rows loaded |

These are acceptance criteria. A build that misses them has not met the requirement, however complete the feature list.

### 6.6 Every complex feature explains itself in-product

Variants, category trees, and completeness are unfamiliar to someone arriving from Monday. Each gets:

- A one-sentence "what this is" at the point of first encounter.
- A concrete "why you'd use this" example drawn from the workspace's own starter preset — for a Campaign type, the example is regional variants, not abstract terminology.
- A dismissible-forever affordance, per-concept, per-user.

Documentation is not a substitute. If the explanation only exists in a help center, it does not count as shipped.

---

## 7. What Makes This Not Just Another Clone

Stated plainly, for the team and for positioning:

**Strata is the first work-management tool that treats complex hierarchical data modeling as a core, easy-to-use primitive** — rather than ignoring it (Monday, ClickUp), making it developer-only (Jira admin), or making it powerful but administratively punishing (Akeneo).

The concrete claims behind that sentence:

| Claim | Monday | ClickUp | Jira | Akeneo | Strata |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reusable typed schema across boards | ✗ | Partial | Admin-only | ✓ | ✓ non-technical |
| Multi-parent classification trees | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Field inheritance / variants | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Completeness scoring | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Spreadsheet-grade bulk editing | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | Partial | ✓ |
| Set up by a non-technical user | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |

The defensible position is the **last row combined with the middle four**. Any single row is copyable. Monday could add a completeness score in a quarter. What is hard to copy is a data model designed for inheritance and multi-tree classification from the schema up, wrapped in an interface a marketing ops lead sets up herself in an afternoon — because retrofitting that model onto a flat-board product is a rewrite, and adding approachability to Akeneo is a decade of accumulated admin surface.

**What this is not:** "Jira with different colors." "Monday with custom fields." If a demo can be summarized either way, the demo led with the wrong thing. Lead with the grid, on 300 rows, doing a bulk edit with preview and undo.

---

## 8. Success Metrics

| Metric | Target | How measured |
|---|---|---|
| **Activation — schema created** | 60% of new workspaces create ≥ 1 custom Item Type within 24h | Product analytics, workspace-level funnel |
| **Activation — time to first Item Type** | Median ≤ 2 min from "New Item Type" click | Instrumented timer, click to first item created |
| **Differentiator adoption** | 40% of active workspaces use ≥ 1 of {variants, custom tree, bulk edit > 20 items} within 14 days | Feature-event tracking |
| **Grid engagement** | 50% of weekly-active workspaces perform ≥ 1 bulk operation per week | Change-set events where `item_count > 1` |
| **Bulk trust** | Undo rate on bulk operations < 10% | Undo events ÷ committed bulk change sets. High undo = bad preview. |
| **Import success** | 80% of started imports reach commit | Import funnel: upload → map → dry-run → commit |
| **Retention** | 40% of workspaces active in week 4 (≥ 3 active days) | Cohort retention |
| **Performance SLO** | 99% of filtered view loads under 300 ms p95 | Server-side traces, alerting on breach |
| **Concept comprehension** | ≥ 4/5 usability participants correctly explain what a variant is after 15 min unaided use | Moderated sessions, pre-launch |
| **Business** | 15 paying workspaces within 90 days of pricing launch | Stripe |

The two that matter most for the thesis are **time to first Item Type** and **differentiator adoption**. Strong retention with near-zero differentiator adoption means users have adopted a slower Monday, and the strategy is wrong.

---

## 9. Assumptions & Risks

| # | Assumption / Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The grid is the hardest thing in the product.** Spreadsheet-grade editing — clipboard interop, rectangular selection, fill-down, undo over bulk ops, virtualization — is routinely underestimated by an order of magnitude. | **High** | Build the grid first, before trees and variants. Timebox a spike in week 1 on clipboard + selection + virtualization specifically. Use TanStack Table + TanStack Virtual rather than writing selection/virtualization from scratch. If the spike slips, cut Board view from MVP before cutting grid fidelity. |
| 2 | **Three hierarchy axes may be one too many to teach.** Work hierarchy + trees + variants is a lot of conceptual load for a Monday switcher. | **High** | The §4.6 constraint (no variants inside the work hierarchy) exists to reduce interaction between axes. Test comprehension in usability sessions before build completes. If users conflate axes, consider hiding variants behind an opt-in per Item Type. |
| 3 | **"Saved views per audience" is not a security boundary in v1.** Field subsetting in a shared view controls presentation. A Guest with API access could read fields the view hides. | **High** | Say so explicitly in-product wherever a view is shared externally. Ship real field-level permissions in Phase 2 (already listed). Until then, gate Guest API access off entirely. Do not let sales imply otherwise. |
| 4 | JSONB + projection-index field storage may not hold at the stated filter performance targets under real-world field counts. | Medium | Load-test at 100k items × 40 fields before feature-complete. Escape hatch (external search index) is designed for in the Tech Spec, not bolted on later. |
| 5 | The wedge persona may be wrong — the sharper pain may be ops/structured-records rather than agencies. | Medium | 10 customer discovery interviews before build starts; the starter presets are cheap to reorder, positioning is not. |
| 6 | Variant inheritance introduces a class of subtle bugs (stale effective values, propagation races) that are expensive to debug in production. | Medium | Materialize effective values with a deterministic recompute path; property-test inheritance resolution; make "recompute this subtree" an admin-visible action. |
| 7 | Competitors ship a lookalike feature. Monday adding "connected boards + rollups" narrows the gap. | Medium | The moat is the combination, not any one feature. Ship the full set quickly; do not spend MVP time on parity features. |
| 8 | Free MVP with no billing means no signal on willingness to pay. | Low | Structure Stripe in from day one (Phase 2 item 12); run pricing conversations with design partners in parallel with the build. |

---

## 10. Open Questions

- [ ] **Pricing model.** Per-seat is conventional, but Strata's value scales with item count and schema complexity, not headcount. Per-seat with an item ceiling? Worth deciding before the Stripe work, not after.
- [ ] **Guest seats — free or paid?** Agency use cases invite many low-touch client guests. Charging per guest kills the wedge; not charging invites abuse.
- [ ] **Does v1 need comments?** Deliberately out of scope above, which also removes @-mentions from v1 notifications. Guest approval workflows arguably require both. Decide before build — retrofitting threaded comments into the item panel is not trivial.
- [ ] **Item Type change management.** When an Item Type changes, do existing items migrate immediately, lazily, or on explicit user action? §4.1 assumes immediate with a preview. Confirm this holds at 50k items.
- [ ] **How many custom trees is "at least one"?** v1 caps at built-in + 1 to prove the model. Is that a real product or an obvious limitation to a user who wanted three?
- [ ] **Self-serve or design-partner launch?** The concept load argues for hand-held onboarding with 5–10 design partners first. That changes what the launch checklist optimizes for.
- [ ] **Undo window length.** 60s toast + 24h from the activity feed is proposed. Is 24h enough for someone who discovers a bad import on Monday morning?
